store.py:76-99: run_memory_call submits func via loop.run_in_executor to a process-wide ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) (lines 80-85, guarded by a lock). One worker draining the executor's FIFO queue gives one-at-a-time, submission-order execution; run_in_executor submits synchronously at call time. Absolute-claim input traced: a caller cancelled while its work item is queued behind a held call. asyncio wraps the concurrent future with wrap_future/_chain_future, and cancelling it calls Future.cancel() on the pending work item. That succeeds, so the item is dropped and never runs. Second input: caller cancelled after the call started. Future.cancel() returns False for a running item, so the function runs to completion on the worker while later items wait in the queue behind it. Third input: calls from two event loops (server and CLI). The executor is module-level and shared, so ordering and serialization still hold across loops; only submission order between loops is by wall-clock submit. Exceptions raised by func are set on the concurrent future and re-raised unchanged through the asyncio future. All four docstring assertions hold.

store.py:80-85 builds the executor with max_workers=1, and run_memory_call (88-99) submits via loop.run_in_executor to it. Input traced: code on the worker thread drives the coroutine with asyncio.run(run_memory_call(f)). That creates a loop on the worker thread, so get_running_loop() at line 98 succeeds. run_in_executor then queues f behind the currently running task, which is the caller itself on the sole worker. The caller blocks in the loop awaiting a future that only the busy worker could complete, so it waits forever. If no coroutine is driven there, get_running_loop() raises RuntimeError, but in that case the call never reaches the executor. The docstring's claim holds for every path that reaches the executor.
